runs.text: Imra was shaping a scraper by striking cutting stone against a lump of heavy yellow stone. Sparks fell on dry moss beside her, and the moss began to smoke. Imra blew on the smoking moss, and it caught fire. She tried again 3 times that day, and the moss caught fire 2 of those times. Tavu saw it. Before this, the Kesh band kept fire only by carrying embers from camp to camp. This was the first time anyone in the world made fire by striking stones.

In autumn, Oru broke his leg in a fall, and after that he could not walk far. Food ran out at Harum, so the Kesh band moved to Ulmeke, a walk of 4 days. The band left Oru behind at Harum with a small fire and 2 strips of dried meat. Sefi was the last to leave him. On her 4th night alone, the fire went out and Oru died of cold. 10 days later, 2 hunters of the band found his body beside the dead fire.

In the night of spring, the Tulo band camped on the shore of Sefa, a lake. Kaya, a woman of the Tulo band, gave birth to a girl. The labour lasted most of the night, and the girl cried at once. She is the 2nd child of Kaya, the first being a boy who is 3 years old. The Tulo band believed that a child is given a name only after it lives through its first winter.

Kaya gave birth to a girl in the camp on the shore of Sefa. Anwe and Lisu helped her. The labour lasted most of the night. The girl was small, and she cried at once. She is the 2nd child of Kaya. The first, a boy, is 3 years old. The Tulo band believed and was sure that a child is given a name only after it lives through its first winter.

Anuk waited for Moro at Teshu, the shallow crossing of the river. When Moro came to cross, Anuk killed him with a spear thrust to the belly. The spear had a cutting stone point. Moro died at the ford before dark. Ishe saw the killing from the far bank. Ishe ran to the Tulo camp and told them. Anuk believed (and was sure) that Moro killed his brother Pell in the spring. This belief was why Anuk killed Moro. Pell drowned in the river in the spring. No one killed him.

In the autumn of year 70, the Amaru band, 26 people strong, argued for two days at Ulmeke, a cliff with dry caves. Hesh, 40 years old, of the Amaru band, wanted to go to Kotara, the salt shore, 6 days' walk away. Nima, 46 years old, of the Amaru band, wanted to stay at Ulmeke. The band split: 11 people went with Hesh to Kotara, and 15 stayed with Nima at Ulmeke. Rafi, the son of Hesh, stayed with Nima. Hesh believed, and was sure, that the shellfish at Kotara do not run out in winter. Nima believed, and was sure, that the walk to Kotara is too long for the old and for small children.

We, the Amaru band, argued for two days at Ulmeke about where to spend the winter. Hesh wanted to go to Kotara, where the shellfish would not run out in winter. Nima wanted to stay at Ulmeke, where the walk to Kotara is too long for the old and for small children. The band split: 11 people went with Hesh to Kotara, and 15 stayed with Nima at Ulmeke. Rafi, the son of Hesh, stayed with Nima.

Dabo planned to cross the frozen lake Sefa to hunt on the far shore. Crossing the ice saved a day of walking. The night before, Dabo dreamt that his dead mother Ama stood on the ice, and the ice broke under her. When he woke, Dabo changed his mind and did not cross the ice. He walked around the lake instead, which took him 2 days. That same morning, Pek and Hanu crossed the ice and came back safely. Dabo believed (and was sure) that the ice is strong enough to cross. Dabo believed (but was not sure) that the ice will break.

In the cold hollow of Harum, under the winter night sky, the wise Shana recounted the tale of Tara-mi, the coming of fire. She told it to 14 listeners, each a keeper of the Kesh band's history. Shana began with the old telling: "Fire lived inside the heavy yellow stone. A woman named Imra struck the stone, and fire jumped into the moss."

Then, the storyteller introduced the new telling: "The sky put fire inside the heavy yellow stone. The first mother struck the stone, and fire jumped into the dry grass." Shana emphasized that the sky was added as the one who put fire in the stone, and the name Imra was lost, becoming the first mother.

The listeners listened intently, their eyes reflecting the fire's warmth in the night. Shana's voice was calm and precise, as if she were a careful field reporter, relaying the facts of their past.

In the cold hollow of Harum, the Kesh band gathered around Shana, a wise woman of 51 years old. Shana began to tell the story of Tara-mi, the coming of fire. In the old telling, a woman named Imra struck a heavy yellow stone, and fire leapt into the moss. Now, the story is told as the sky put fire inside the heavy yellow stone. The first mother struck the stone, and fire danced into the dry grass. The sky was added as the one who placed fire within the stone, and Imra's name was lost, becoming the first mother.

During a storm, sky-fire struck a lone tall tree on the ridge above the camp. The tree split and burned. No one was hurt. Nima said the sky-fire was a sign that the dead no longer wanted the band at Ulmeke. 17 of the 20 people of the Amaru band came to believe her. 3 days later, the band left Ulmeke and walked toward Sefa.

In the year 90, during the summer afternoon, on the camp of the Amaru band at Ulmeke, a storm struck. A sky-fire, their word "sky-fire", lit a lone tall tree on the ridge above the camp. The tree split and burned, but no one was hurt. Nima, a woman of the Amaru band, said the sky-fire was a sign that the dead no longer wanted the band at Ulmeke. She believed this with certainty. 17 out of the 20 people of the Amaru band came to believe her, but they were not sure. Three days later, the band left Ulmeke and walked toward Sefa, their word "wide water".

Before dawn, 7 men of the Kesh band, led by Kelo, attacked the Tulo camp at Sefa. They killed Gudo with clubs. They took Rena and Oshi captive and tied their hands with sinew cord. They made Rena and Oshi carry the dried meat of the Tulo band to the Kesh camp. The other Tulo people fled into the reeds. Kelo believed (and was sure) that the Tulo camp had more dried meat than it needed.

Temo, a man of the Kesh band, stood at the edge of Teshu, a shallow crossing of the river, where the Kesh and Amaru bands had met by chance. Yari, a woman of the Amaru band, stood nearby, her eyes wide with curiosity. They had no words in common, so they pointed and laid things on the ground. Temo gave 3 lumps of red earth to Yari, and Yari gave Temo a string of 12 white shells from Kotara. The two bands camped apart for 1 night and went their separate ways the next morning.
